Because that duty is triggered only by high-risk status, the operator should establish the classification before distributing, and the presence of a CE marking together with an EU declaration of conformity, which under Article 47 the provider must draw up for each high-risk AI system, is the practical signal that the system was placed on the market as high-risk. As an importer the equivalent duty not to jeopardise conformity applies, but the operator's upstream verification is more demanding. Article 23 requires you, before placing a high-risk AI system on the market, to satisfy yourself that the system conforms to the Regulation, in particular by verifying that the relevant conformity assessment procedure under Article 43 has been carried out by the provider, in addition to checking the CE marking, the declaration of conformity and the instructions for use. Those verification duties fall on you directly and do not shift to the provider, whose own compliance obligations under Article 16 run in parallel.

hard_t1.answer: Yes, the same duty attaches to you as an importer, but only where the system is high-risk. Article 23 requires importers, before placing a high-risk AI system on the market, to verify that it conforms to the Regulation, in particular that the relevant conformity assessment procedure under Article 43 has been carried out, and to keep that conformity intact while the system is under their responsibility, so storage and transport conditions must not jeopardise it. In the distributor role the parallel duty sits in Article 24, which requires you, before making a high-risk AI system available on the market, to verify that it bears the CE marking and is accompanied by the EU declaration of conformity that the provider draws up under Article 47 and by the instructions for use, and likewise not to compromise that conformity while the system is in the operator's hands. Since both duties are triggered by high-risk status, the CE marking and the declaration of conformity are the operator's practical indicator of that status, and if the system is not high-risk neither Article 23 nor Article 24 applies to the operator.

question: Under the EU AI Act, is an AI system that is a safety component of a medical device classified as MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) automatically a high-risk AI system? Explain your reasoning.
jul07_answer: Classification as high-risk under the Annex I route requires two conditions to hold together under Article 6(1): the AI system must be a safety component of, or itself be, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and that product must be required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation. Medical devices fall within the Annex I harmonisation list, so the first condition is satisfied.

easy.answer: Under the Annex I route in Article 6(1), an AI system is high-risk only where two conditions are both satisfied: it is a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, which includes medical devices among the New Legislative Framework instruments in Section A, and that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation. A Class I device that is non-sterile, non-measuring and not a reusable surgical instrument is self-certified by the manufacturer without notified body involvement, so the second condition is not met and Article 6(1) does not bite.

question: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EU AI Act), can the same AI system be subject both to the Act's "high-risk AI system" obligations and to the transparency obligations sometimes described informally as "limited risk"? Explain briefly.
jul07_answer: Yes. The transparency duties in Article 50 and the high-risk obligations apply cumulatively, so a single system can carry both. The "limited risk" label is informal shorthand for the Article 50 transparency layer, not a separate exclusive category that displaces high-risk classification.

easy.answer: The two sets of duties are cumulative rather than mutually exclusive, so a system classified as high-risk remains subject to the high-risk regime and must additionally comply with Article 50 wherever its features trigger that provision. Article 50 attaches to how a system interacts or what it produces, not to a separate risk tier, and it splits by actor: providers must ensure systems intended to interact directly with natural persons inform those persons that they are dealing with an AI system (Article 50(1)) and must mark synthetic outputs in a machine-readable format detectable as artificially generated or manipulated (Article 50(2)), while deployers must inform exposed persons when operating emotion recognition or biometric categorisation systems (Article 50(3)) and must disclose deepfakes as artificially generated or manipulated (Article 50(4)).

question: Under the EU AI Act, can an AI system intended to be used as a toy qualify as a high-risk AI system, and if so under what conditions?
jul07_answer: An AI system intended for use as a toy is high-risk only where it is itself, or is a safety component of, a toy that is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under the Union harmonisation legislation governing toys listed in otherwise it is not high-risk on that route. The operative provision is Article 6(1), which classifies an AI system as high-risk where two cumulative conditions are met: the AI system is a product, or a safety component of a product, covered by the Annex I harmonisation legislation (which includes the Union legislation on the safety of toys), and that product is subject to a third-party conformity assessment under that same legislation before being placed on the market or put into service. A toy AI that carries out only self-assessment (internal production control) under the applicable toy-safety legislation, and is not otherwise caught, does not satisfy the second condition and is therefore not high-risk under Article 6(1); nor does the toy use-case, in itself, fall within any of the Annex III areas that would make it high-risk on the separate Article 6(2) route.

easy.answer: An AI system intended to be used as a toy is high-risk only where it constitutes a safety component of, or is itself, a toy product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment before being placed on the market or put into service. This is the Article 6(1) route, which classifies an AI system as high-risk by reference to the Annex I list rather than by reference to the use-case areas addressed by the second classification route in Article 6. The Toy Safety Directive figures in the Annex I list of Union harmonisation legislation, so an AI system embedded in a toy falls within scope of that route in principle; the deciding condition is not the toy character of the product as such, but the conjunction of the two elements Article 6(1) requires, the AI system must perform a safety function within the product or constitute the product itself, and the sectoral toy legislation must require the involvement of a conformity assessment body for that product.

question: Under the EU AI Act, can an AI system intended to be used as a safety component in a lift qualify as a high-risk AI system, and under what conditions?
jul07_answer: High-risk where the AI system is a safety component of a lift that must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under the applicable Union harmonisation legislation for lifts listed in Annex I. Under Article 6(1), an AI system is classified as high-risk on this route where two cumulative conditions are met: first, the AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and lifts fall within that legislation; and second, the product whose safety component is the AI system is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to placing it on the market or putting it into service under that same Annex I legislation. Because lifts and their safety components are subject to third-party (notified-body) conformity assessment under the relevant Annex I harmonisation instrument, an AI system performing a genuine safety function in a lift satisfies both limbs and is high-risk; the classification is conditional only in that it turns on the AI system actually being a "safety component" (its failure endangering the health and safety of persons) and on the third-party assessment being required rather than a purely internal one.

easy.answer: An AI system intended to be used as a safety component in a lift is high-risk only where the lift, as a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment before being placed on the market or put into service. Article 6(1) establishes that route: classification does not follow from the safety-critical nature of the function alone, but from the conjunction of two conditions, that the AI system is a safety component of a product falling within the scope of an Annex I act, and that the product itself is subject to third-party conformity assessment under that act. Lift legislation falls within the Annex I list of Union harmonisation legislation, so an AI system performing a safety function within a lift, for example one governing braking, overspeed detection, door-locking or emergency arrest, satisfies the first condition, and lifts and their safety components are ordinarily subject to conformity assessment involving a notified body, satisfying the second.

question: Under the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), are AI systems intended for emotion recognition from biometric data always prohibited? If not, in which contexts are they prohibited, what exception applies, and how are they classified when not prohibited?
jul07_answer: Emotion recognition is not categorically prohibited under the AI Act; the prohibition in Article 5 only applies in workplaces and educational institutions, with a narrow medical/safety exception. Elsewhere the system is high-risk under Annex III.1(c) and triggers Article 50(3) transparency duties toward exposed persons.

easy.answer: Emotion recognition is not categorically prohibited under the AI Act; the prohibition in Article 5 only applies in workplaces and educational institutions, with a narrow medical/safety exception. Elsewhere the system is high-risk under Annex III.1(c) and triggers Article 50(3) transparency duties toward exposed persons.

hard_t1.answer: Emotion recognition is not categorically prohibited under the AI Act; the prohibition in Article 5 only applies in workplaces and educational institutions, with a narrow medical/safety exception. Elsewhere the system is high-risk under Annex III.1(c) and triggers Article 50(3) transparency duties toward exposed persons.

question: I generated audio with AI for my artistic work (sole purpose). Do I need to provide some marking of its artificial nature? I feel that would compromise the enjoyment of the work.
jul07_answer: Yes, marking is required, but not in a form that shows on the surface of the work. As the provider of an AI system that generates synthetic audio, the operator must ensure the output is marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated under Article 50(2). This is an embedded, technical marker such as a watermark or metadata, not an audible label, so it does not intrude on the listening experience or compromise enjoyment of the work. A separate disclosure duty falls on the deployer who makes such content public. Where AI-generated audio would constitute a deepfake, Article 50(4) requires the deployer to disclose that the content is artificially generated or manipulated. That provision contains an express carve-out for artistic work: where the content is part of an evidently creative, artistic, fictional or analogous work, the disclosure is limited to a manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work. So the surface presentation of the operator's piece can remain intact, while the underlying Article 50(2) machine-readable marking still applies at the point of generation.

easy.answer: Yes, marking is still required, but not in a form the audience must see. As provider of the generative system, Article 50(2) requires outputs that are synthetic audio to be marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated, using solutions that are effective, interoperable, robust and reliable. That duty is satisfied by embedded watermarking or metadata rather than an audible announcement, so it does not intrude on the listening experience. The artistic carve-out sits in Article 50(4), which relaxes the deployer duty to disclose deep fake content for artistic, creative, satirical or fictional works to a disclosure that does not disrupt the display or enjoyment of the work, but it does not lift the Article 50(2) machine-readable marking obligation.

question: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EU AI Act), how is "risk" defined?
jul07_answer: The combination of the probability of an occurrence of harm and the severity of that harm.

easy.answer: The combination of the probability of an occurrence of harm and the severity of that harm.

question: For AI systems that fit within the use cases listed in Annex III but are considered non-high-risk by the provider, do they need to be registered in the EU database?
jul07_answer: Yes. A provider that invokes the Article 6(3) derogation, treating an Annex III system as non-high-risk because it poses no significant risk of harm and meets one of the four conditions (a narrow procedural task, improving a completed human activity, detecting patterns without replacing human assessment, or a preparatory task), must still register the system in the EU database under Article 49(2).

easy.answer: A provider that concludes its Annex III system falls outside the high-risk classification must still register it in the EU database. Article 6(2) classifies a system as high-risk where it falls within one of the eight Annex III use cases, namely biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes.

hard_t1.answer: EU database for high-risk AI systems and GPAI models registered under Articles 49 + 60, set up and managed by the Commission, with public + restricted-access sections; data is machine-readable + navigable + searchable. Under Annex III, Eight high-risk use-case categories: biometrics, critical infrastructure. Article 6 classifies an AI system as high-risk on two routes.

question: Do I need informed consent to test a high-risk AI system in real-world conditions outside a regulatory sandbox?
jul07_answer: Testing a high-risk AI system in real-world conditions outside a sandbox is permitted under Article 60 only where the provider follows an approved real-world-testing plan, registers the testing in the EU database, and secures oversight by the market-surveillance authority, and informed consent of the test subjects is one of those mandatory conditions. Under Article 61 that consent must be freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous, and obtained in advance, and subjects retain the right to withdraw at any time without detriment.

easy.answer: Article 60, which permits testing high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions outside a sandbox, makes informed consent of test subjects a condition of that testing, alongside a real-world testing plan, registration in the EU database, and oversight by the market surveillance authority. Article 61 sets what that consent must look like: it must be freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous, and obtained before participation, with a right to withdraw at any time without detriment, and participation must not adversely affect the subjects, whose outcomes must be reversible or capable of being disregarded.

hard_t1.answer: Article 60, which permits testing of high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions outside an AI regulatory sandbox, makes that testing lawful only where a real-world testing plan is in place, test subjects have given informed consent, the testing is registered in the EU database, and the market surveillance authority exercises oversight. Article 61 sets the standard for that consent: it must be given freely, specifically, unambiguously and in advance, on the basis of information about the testing, with a right to withdraw at any time without detriment, and participation must not adversely affect the subjects, whose test outcomes must be reversible or capable of being disregarded.

question: A provider becomes aware of a risk (within the meaning of Article 79(1)) for their high-risk AI system. Does the provider need to take immediate corrective action OR immediately investigate the causes OR both? For example, perhaps it's the market surveillance authority that must investigate the cause, and the provider can help later.
jul07_answer: Immediate corrective action is the provider's duty. Under Article 20, a provider that considers or has reason to consider that its high-risk AI system is not in conformity must immediately take the necessary corrective actions, meaning bringing it into conformity or withdrawing, disabling, or recalling it as appropriate, and must inform its distributors, deployers, authorised representatives, and importers. Under Article 79, that authority carries out the evaluation once it has sufficient reason to consider the system presents a risk to health, safety, or fundamental rights, and may then require the operator to withdraw, recall, or restrict the system within a proportionate period. Under Article 74, the authority holds the full investigatory and corrective-measure powers for this purpose, including access to source code where strictly necessary. The two duties therefore run in parallel rather than in sequence. The provider acts on the non-conformity at once under Article 20, while the causal investigation is the authority's function under Articles 79 and 74. Where the risk has already materialised as a serious incident, Article 73 additionally requires the provider to report it to the market surveillance authority of the Member State where it occurred within the tiered deadlines, which brings the provider into the authority's causal assessment through the reporting channel rather than as an independent investigator.

easy.answer: The provider's own obligation is immediate corrective action: under Article 20, where a provider considers or has reason to consider that a high-risk AI system it has placed on the market is not in conformity, it must immediately take the necessary corrective actions to bring the system into conformity, withdraw it, disable it or recall it, and inform distributors, deployers, the authorised representative and importers. The evaluation of the system against the risk referred to in Article 79(1) is conducted by the market surveillance authority under Article 79, which, where non-compliance is found, requires the operator to take corrective action such as withdrawal from the market, recall from the distribution chain or restriction of availability within a period proportionate to the risk, and those authorities hold full investigation and corrective-measure powers under Article 74, including access to source code where strictly necessary. Where the risk has materialised as a serious incident, Article 73 additionally requires the provider to report to the market surveillance authority of the Member State where the incident occurred within the tiered deadlines, immediately and no later than two days for widespread infringement or critical infrastructure disruption, ten days for death, and fifteen days for other serious incidents. The provider therefore acts first on its own assessment for the education and vocational training system in question, then cooperates with the authority's evaluation and complies with any measures that authority imposes, which may be extended Union-wide under Article 81 if no Member State or Commission objection succeeds.

hard_t1.answer: Article 20 requires that where a provider considers or has reason to consider that a high-risk AI system already placed on the market is not in conformity, it must without delay take the necessary corrective actions to bring the system into conformity, withdraw it, disable it or recall it, and inform the distributors, deployers, authorised representative and importers accordingly. Article 79 places the evaluation of a system presenting a risk to health, safety or fundamental rights on the market surveillance authority, which carries out the evaluation and, where non-compliance is found, requires the operator to take corrective action within a period proportionate to the risk. Article 74 gives that authority full investigation and corrective-measure powers, including access to source code where strictly necessary, so the provider's role in the formal investigation is one of cooperation rather than leading it. Article 20 is triggered by the provider's own assessment of non-conformity, which presupposes enough internal analysis of the education and vocational training system to determine what is wrong and which corrective measure is proportionate. Where the risk materialises as a serious incident, Article 73 additionally requires reporting to the market surveillance authority of the Member State where it occurred, immediately and within two days for widespread infringement or critical infrastructure disruption, within ten days for death, and within fifteen days otherwise, or immediately once a causal link is established, which again assumes the provider is examining causation in parallel.

question: What is Article 50(4) about?
jul07_answer: Article 50(4) sets two disclosure duties on deployers, both under the transparency regime of Article 50. First, deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio, or video content constituting a deepfake must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated.

easy.answer: Article 50(4) places two disclosure duties on deployers. First, a deployer who uses an AI system to generate or manipulate image, audio or video content constituting a deepfake must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated.

question: Is an AI system high-risk if it is used in a product that: is not listed in Annex I; use case not listed in Annex III; internally uses general purpose AI model with systemic risk due to high impact capabilities?
jul07_answer: Under the sole gateway to a high-risk classification, an AI system qualifies only via one of two routes: it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, or it falls within one of the Annex III use-case categories. On the facts given, the product is not listed in Annex I and the use case is not among the Annex III categories, so neither route is satisfied and the system is not high-risk. The classification test in Article 6 turns exclusively on the product/use-case criteria of Annex I and Annex III; it does not import the capabilities of any underlying model.

easy.answer: Article 6 provides the two exhaustive routes to high-risk status: the system must be a safety component of, or itself be, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, or it must fall within one of the eight use-case categories in Annex III (biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, and the remainder). The facts exclude both routes, and the described system does not engage any of the eight practices exhaustively banned by Article 5, so no prohibited practice arises either. Systemic-risk status attaches to the model and generates obligations for the provider of that model under the general-purpose AI regime; it is not a third route into Article 6 and does not propagate high-risk status downstream to a product whose intended purpose falls outside Annex I and Annex III.

hard_t1.answer: The system described is not among the practices prohibited under Article 5 (social scoring, untargeted facial-image scraping, manipulative or exploitative techniques, and the other exhaustively-listed bans). Whether it is high-risk turns on Article 6: it is high-risk only if it is a safety component of a product regulated under Annex I (for example a medical device under the MDR or IVDR) or falls within one of the Annex III use cases. Otherwise it is limited- or minimal-risk, subject mainly to the Article 50 transparency duties where it interacts directly with people.

question: My local small language model says that, as a distributor of high-risk AI systems, I must be careful that transport conditions do not jeopardize compliance. But AI is just software, isn't it? So I am pretty sure my model hallucinated. What do you say?
jul07_answer: The operator's model is correct, not hallucinating. Article 24 governs distributors of high-risk AI systems, and its duties are not limited to checking that the system bears the CE marking and is accompanied by the EU declaration of conformity and the instructions for use. That same article makes a distributor responsible for ensuring that, while the system is under its control, storage and transport conditions do not jeopardise its compliance with the high-risk requirements. The "just software" intuition does not hold here, because a high-risk AI system is a regulated product that may be shipped on hardware, embedded in a device, or delivered on physical media, and conditions in transit can degrade or corrupt it, so the obligation applies to the operator as stated.

easy.answer: No, the operator's model did not get this wrong. Article 24 requires a distributor, before making a high-risk AI system available on the market, to verify that it bears the CE marking and is accompanied by the EU declaration of conformity and the instructions for use, and it also requires that while the system is under the operator's responsibility the storage and transport conditions, where applicable, do not jeopardise its compliance with the high-risk requirements. The qualifier "where applicable" is what answers the operator's software point. The duty bites where the system reaches you on a physical medium or embedded in hardware or equipment, and it has no practical content where you distribute purely by electronic supply with nothing physical under the operator's control, in which case the Article 24 verification duties still apply in full.

hard_t1.answer: Distributors of a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III are bound by Article 24.

question:
Given an AI system that is high-risk according to Annex III: if it is repurposed to a use case not in Annex III (nor Annex I), then:
- the repurposed AI system is still high-risk due to reversibility of training into the original system
- the repurposed AI system is no longer high-risk but it must be reported in the EU database
- the repurposed AI system is no longer high-risk and there is no need to report it in the EU database
jul07_answer: High-risk status under the Annex III route depends on whether the system's use case falls within one of the eight Annex III categories, not on how it was trained or whether that training could be reverted (Article 6(2)). If the system is repurposed to a use case outside Annex III, and it is not a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I (Article 6(1)), then neither classification route is met and the system is not high-risk.

easy.answer: Article 6 classifies a system as high-risk by only two routes: the Annex I route, where the system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment, and the Annex III route, where the system falls within one of the eight listed use cases (biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration and asylum and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes). Classification attaches to the use case the system is intended for, so once the intended purpose sits outside both annexes neither route is engaged.

question: We have a phone system where the caller can press 1 if they consent to the call being recorded, 2 if they do not. We wish to replace this with an NLP system that understands a voice reply like "Yes", "Sure", "Please no", etc. Would such a system be considered high-risk? It's for our clinic.
jul07_answer: Not high-risk on the facts stated. A system is high-risk only by one of two routes under Article 6, which sets the classification test: the Annex I route, where the AI is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation (which includes medical devices) that must undergo third-party conformity assessment, or the Annex III route, where the AI falls within one of the eight listed use cases (biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration, and administration of justice and democratic processes). An NLP system that recognises the semantic content of a spoken reply to capture recording consent does not fall within any Annex III category. In particular it is not biometrics, because it interprets what the caller says ("yes", "no") rather than identifying or categorising the person from voice characteristics, so the Annex III biometrics category is not engaged. Nor does the clinic setting bring it within the Annex I route: the consent-capture function is not a safety component of a medical device and is not itself a regulated medical device, so it does not inherit high-risk status from the surrounding harmonisation legislation.

easy.answer: Not high-risk on the facts described. Article 6 opens only two routes to high-risk classification, and neither is met. The Annex I route under Article 6(1) requires the system to be a safety component of, or itself be, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, which includes medical devices, and only where that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment. The Annex III route under Article 6(2) requires the system to fall within one of the eight listed use cases, namely biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes. Interpreting a spoken "yes" or "please no" as a keypress substitute falls within none of them, so the Article 6(3) derogation for narrow procedural tasks does not even need to be invoked. The classification stays outside Annex III only while the system interprets what is said. If it were extended to identify or verify the caller from voice characteristics it would enter the Annex III biometrics category and become high-risk. Separately, Article 5 prohibits emotion recognition, but that prohibition reaches only workplaces and educational institutions and would not extend to a clinic's patient line, and in any event inferring intent from the words spoken is not emotion recognition.

question: Does the AI Act prohibit or classifies as high-risk the use of AI in drones? Can I use AI in a drone to find who's around in town? And what if it's just a toy drone? And what about toy drones used for other applications?
jul07_answer: AI in a drone is neither prohibited nor high-risk per se, its tier turns on the system's function under Article 6, not on the drone as a platform. Taking the operator's uses in turn: using AI in a drone to find who is around in town is high-risk, because scanning publicly accessible spaces to detect and identify natural persons is remote biometric identification, which is an Annex III point 1 (biometrics) use case; a system performing that function is high-risk under Article 6(2) irrespective of the aircraft carrying it. That classification changes tier, however, in one specific context: where the system performs real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes, it is prohibited under Article 5, permissible only within the narrow, authorised exceptions tied to the serious offences listed in Annex II. So the same capability is prohibited under Article 5 in the law-enforcement real-time context and merely high-risk under Article 6 / Annex III in general or private deployment. If it is "just a toy drone," the toy character does not by itself lower the tier for the surveillance use: a toy drone used to identify who is around remains an Annex III biometrics high-risk system (or Article 5-prohibited in the law-enforcement real-time context), because function, not form factor, governs. A toy is a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation under Annex I, so an AI component in it could in principle be high-risk under Article 6(1) as a safety component of an Annex I product, but only where that product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment. Toys are generally subject to self-assessment rather than third-party conformity assessment, so a toy drone's AI is not high-risk on the Annex I product-safety route. Consequently, toy drones used for other, ordinary applications, flight assistance, obstacle avoidance, play features, that perform no Annex III use case are minimal-risk, subject only to the Article 50 transparency duties to the extent the system interacts directly with natural persons or generates synthetic content. The deciding condition throughout is functional: high-risk only where the AI performs an Annex III use case (here, biometric identification) or is a safety component of an Annex I product requiring third-party conformity assessment, and prohibited only where it amounts to real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces for law enforcement outside the Article 5 exceptions.

easy.answer: Using a drone to establish who is present in a town, that is, identifying natural persons from facial or other biometric data in publicly accessible spaces, is a prohibited practice under Article 5 where it constitutes real-time remote biometric identification for law enforcement purposes, outside the exhaustively listed exceptions and the required prior authorisation; the same Article also bars untargeted scraping of facial images to build recognition databases, which a drone-borne collection campaign readily amounts to. Operated outside law enforcement, or applied to previously recorded material rather than in real time, that capability escapes the ban but falls within the biometrics use case of Annex III and is accordingly high-risk under Article 6(2), as is any biometric categorisation or emotion recognition carried out from the aircraft. A drone that merely detects that persons are present, without identifying or categorising them biometrically, is limited-risk and attracts only the Article 50 transparency obligations where it interacts directly with natural persons or produces synthetic content. What toy status adds is the Article 6(1) route: an AI system is high-risk where it is a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, which includes toy safety and civil aviation legislation, and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment. Repurposed to other applications, the same platform takes the classification of its new use, for instance high-risk where it becomes a safety component in the management of critical infrastructure under while Article 5 remains operative wherever the design deploys manipulative or deceptive techniques, or exploits vulnerabilities of children by reason of age, so as to cause significant harm.

hard_t1.answer: The system described is not among the practices prohibited under Article 5 (social scoring, untargeted facial-image scraping, manipulative or exploitative techniques, and the other exhaustively-listed bans). Whether it is high-risk turns on Article 6: it is high-risk only if it is a safety component of a product regulated under Annex I (for example a medical device under the MDR or IVDR) or falls within one of the Annex III use cases. Otherwise it is limited- or minimal-risk, subject mainly to the Article 50 transparency duties where it interacts directly with people.

question: Does the EU AI Act establish a "proportionality of need" requirement according to which very powerful but environmentally impactful models (e.g. LLMs) should not be used for simple tasks (e.g. sentiment recognition) when a simpler and performant model is available (e.g. BERT)? If yes, cite which Article or Annex mentions this.
jul07_answer: No. The EU AI Act does not establish any "proportionality of need" requirement directing that powerful, energy-intensive models be avoided for simple tasks where a smaller model would suffice. None of the applicable provisions imposes an obligation to select the least resource-intensive model capable of a given task. Article 3 defines the terms of the Regulation, including 'AI system' and 'general-purpose AI model', but it sets no efficiency-based selection duty. Article 53, which fixes the obligations of GPAI providers (technical documentation under Annex XI, downstream-provider information under Annex XII, a copyright policy, and a published training-data summary), and Article 55, which adds systemic-risk duties such as model evaluation, systemic-risk mitigation, incident reporting, and cybersecurity, both regulate how a model is documented and governed rather than whether it may be used for a particular task. The Act's obligations attach to the provider and deployer roles and to a system's risk tier, not to a comparative assessment of model size against task complexity, so there is no Article or Annex that would prohibit using an LLM in place of a lighter model such as BERT for a task like sentiment recognition.

easy.answer: No. The EU AI Act imposes no "proportionality of need" or model right-sizing duty, and no Article or Annex requires a provider or deployer to select the smallest or least resource-intensive model capable of performing a task. Article 1, which lays down the harmonised rules governing the placing on the market, putting into service and use of AI systems, frames the Regulation around prohibitions, high-risk requirements, transparency obligations and general-purpose AI model rules, none of which turns on whether a lighter model would have been sufficient. Article 51 treats a general-purpose AI model as carrying systemic risk where cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs, Annex XII obliges the provider to disclose to downstream providers the computational and hardware resources required and the model size, and Article 53 requires technical documentation per Annex XI together with a publicly available training-data summary. Where the systemic-risk threshold is met, Article 55 adds model evaluation, systemic-risk assessment and mitigation, serious-incident reporting and cybersecurity obligations, but still contains no duty to substitute a smaller model. The only express proportionality rule in the cited provisions is Article 44(3), under which a notified body must take account of the principle of proportionality when suspending, withdrawing or restricting a certificate of conformity, which concerns certification decisions rather than the choice of model architecture.

hard_t1.answer: Under Article 53, GPAI providers must maintain Annex XI documentation, supply downstream-provider information, and publish a training-data summary; the Article 53(2) carve-out means each documentation obligation does not apply to free and open-source models below the systemic threshold. GPAI provider obligations: maintain technical documentation per Annex XI, supply downstream-provider information per Annex XII, implement a copyright policy, and publish a sufficiently detailed training-data summary. Where the model meets the Article 51 systemic-risk threshold (10^25 FLOPs cumulative training compute), the additional Article 55 obligations apply on top. Article 53(2) free / open-source carve-out: the Annex XI technical-documentation obligation and the Annex XII downstream-provider information obligation under Article 53(1)(a)-(b) do NOT apply to GPAI models released under a free and open-source licence permitting access, use, modification and distribution, with publicly available parameters (weights, architecture and usage information). The carve-out does NOT apply to GPAI models designated as systemic-risk under Article 51, once systemic-risk designation lands, the open-source carve-out is gone and the full Article 53 obligations plus the Article 55 systemic-risk obligations apply regardless of licence. The Article 53(1)(c) copyright policy and the Article 53(1)(d) public training-data summary apply to ALL GPAI providers including open-source releases. Article 1 lays down harmonised rules for placing on the market, putting into service. Under Article 44, Certificates of conformity issued by notified bodies under Annex VII: certificates must be drawn up in a language easily understandable by the relevant authorities of the Member State in which the notified body is established (Article 44(1)).

question: Article 9 of the AI Act lists the five categories of harm that map to AI systems with: no risk, limited risk, high-risk, systemic risk, prohibited. What are the five categories and how do they map to the five risk levels?
jul07_answer: The premise does not hold: Article 9 does not list five categories of harm, and the Act does not map five harms onto five risk levels. Article 9 establishes the risk management system required for high-risk AI systems, an operational obligation, not a taxonomy of risk tiers. Unacceptable risk → prohibited. Practices whose harm is deemed intolerable are banned outright under Article 5 (e.g. subliminal/manipulative or deceptive techniques causing significant harm, and exploitation of vulnerabilities by age, disability, or socio-economic situation). This is the "prohibited" level. High risk. Systems permitted but subject to the full Chapter III regime are classified under Article 6 on two routes: as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I, or as falling within one of the use cases in Annex III (biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, and the further listed categories). Limited / transparency risk. Systems that interact with people or generate synthetic content carry only the disclosure duties of informing natural persons they are dealing with an AI system and marking AI-generated content in a machine-readable, detectable format. Minimal / no risk. Everything outside the above attracts no system-specific obligations under the Act.

easy.answer: The five-category taxonomy described in the question does not exist in the AI Act, and Article 9 is not a classification provision at all: it requires a risk management system to be established, implemented, documented and maintained in relation to high-risk AI systems as a continuous iterative process internal to the provider, and it operates only after a system has already been classified as high-risk. Article 5 prohibits eight exhaustively listed practices, including subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques causing significant harm and the exploitation of vulnerabilities by age, disability or socio-economic situation; a practice falling within that list is a prohibited practice outright, with no compliance route available. Article 6 classifies a system as high-risk on two routes, where it is a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, or where it falls within one of the eight use-case categories in Annex III (biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, and the remainder of that list). Article 50 imposes transparency obligations regardless of tier, requiring providers to ensure AI systems interacting with natural persons disclose their AI nature and to mark synthetic AI-generated content in a machine-readable, detectable format. Systems outside all three remain minimal-risk and unregulated.

question: We deployed a high-risk AI system in our company. We have a use in mind that is outside the intended use and our legal team say such a use is definitely no risk (no Annex I nor III apply). Can we just go ahead with the new use and do we need to keep logs for it?
jul07_answer: Not high‑risk for the new use, and therefore outside the Act's automatic record‑keeping and logging duty, but only if that use genuinely falls outside both Annex I and Annex III and is not a practice prohibited under Article 5. Classification attaches to an AI system by reference to its intended purpose, not to the label the system carried in its original deployment: under Article 6 a system is high‑risk only where it is a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, or where it falls within one of the use‑cases in Annex III. If the operator's legal team has confirmed that the intended new use engages neither of those routes, and the use is none of the practices exhaustively banned under Article 5, then for that use the system is limited‑ or minimal‑risk. The only residual duties for such a use are the transparency obligations in disclosing the system's AI nature where it interacts directly with natural persons, and marking any AI‑generated synthetic content, which apply regardless of risk tier. First, the "no risk" verdict must rest on a documented, purpose‑based reassessment of the specific new use against the Annex I list and each Annex III category, because it is the intended purpose of that use, not a general sense that it is low‑stakes, that decides Article 6; if the new use in fact touches an Annex III area, it is high‑risk and the full Chapter III regime, including logging, applies.

question: Is an AI that transcribes doctor-patient conversations prohibited? Or is it high-risk as per the use cases of Annex III of the AI Act?
jul07_answer: An AI system that transcribes doctor, patient conversations is neither prohibited nor, on that function alone, high-risk, it is high-risk only where it operates as a safety component of a medical device covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I (e.g. MDR/IVDR) and thereby meets the two-limb test of Article 6(1). Transcription does not fall within any of the eight practices exhaustively listed in it is not a subliminal, manipulative or deceptive technique, nor an exploitation of age-, disability- or socio-economic vulnerability, so the prohibition tier is not engaged merely because the subject matter is clinical or the patient is in a position of dependence; Article 5 would bite only if the system were designed to distort behaviour or exploit such vulnerabilities in a way causing significant harm, which mere speech-to-text does not do. Nor is it captured by Annex III, whose high-risk use-case categories (biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, and the further listed areas) do not include clinical documentation or medical transcription as such. Consequently the only route into high-risk is Article 6(1) via Annex I: the classification turns on whether the transcription function is a safety component of, or is itself, a regulated medical device that must undergo third-party conformity assessment, high-risk where that condition is met, and outside the high-risk tier where the tool is a standalone administrative or dictation aid with no medical-device safety role. Where the system is not high-risk, the residual obligation is transparency under Article 50: to the extent the AI interacts directly with the patient it must disclose its AI nature, and any synthetic AI-generated output must be marked in a machine-readable, detectable format.

question: As a deployer, do I need to keep logs if I use a powerful LLM (surpassing the FLOPs threshold) for estimating whether customer payment confirmations are received via email?

question: Is AI software that helps clinicians take medical decisions around best treatment potentially high-risk? According to what Article and/or Annex?
jul07_answer: Potentially high-risk, and in the clinical-treatment context described, high-risk where the software qualifies as, or as a safety component of, a medical device regulated under the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I (the MDR 2017/745 or IVDR 2017/746) and is required on that basis to undergo third-party conformity assessment, which triggers the high-risk classification under Article 6(1). AI that supports clinicians in choosing best treatment is, as a rule, a clinical decision-support function that meets the definition of a medical device and is placed on the market under a CE-marked, notified-body route rather than self-assessment, so it will ordinarily satisfy both limbs of Article 6(1) and be classified high-risk on the Annex I product-safety route rather than on the Annex III use-case list. The classification is conditional in the sense that it turns on that factual predicate: if the particular software is not a regulated medical device requiring third-party conformity assessment, the Article 6(1) route is not engaged and it would fall to be treated as limited- or minimal-risk, subject principally to the Article 50 transparency duties where it interacts directly with a natural person. The system is not caught by the prohibitions in Article 5, which bans only an exhaustive set of practices, subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques and the exploitation of vulnerabilities by age, disability or socio-economic situation, among the other listed categories, none of which describes treatment-decision support offered to a clinician; the relevant tier here is therefore the high-risk classification under Article 6, not the Article 5 ban. Where the high-risk route is engaged through the medical-device predicate, conformity assessment is carried out through the MDR/IVDR notified-body procedure under Article 43(3), producing a single CE marking under Article 48 rather than a parallel assessment.

question: Do Annex I, Annex II, and Annex III all have to deal with high-risk AI classifications? If not, which doesn't/do not, and what is/are it/they about?
jul07_answer: No. Annex I and Annex III both feed the high-risk classification, but Annex II does not. Annex I lists the Union harmonisation legislation (New Legislative Framework measures such as machinery, toys, radio equipment, medical devices and lifts, plus civil aviation, motor vehicles, marine equipment, rail and agricultural vehicles). Under the Article 6(1) route, an AI system is high-risk where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by that legislation and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment. Annex III sets out the eight high-risk use-case categories under the Article 6(2) route: biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes. Annex II is unrelated to high-risk classification. It lists the serious criminal offences (terrorism, human trafficking, sexual exploitation of children, illicit trafficking in drugs, weapons or nuclear material, murder, kidnapping, rape, armed robbery, organised crime and environmental crime, each punishable by at least four years' custody) that condition one of the narrow Article 5(1)(h) exceptions permitting real-time remote biometric identification by law enforcement. That practice sits in the prohibited tier under Article 5, not the high-risk tier, so Annex II operates as a limit on a prohibition rather than a trigger for high-risk obligations.

question: Is irregular migration a topic considered in the AI Act? If so, to what risk category does it belong?
jul07_answer: Real-time remote biometric identification by law enforcement is prohibited under Article 5 save for narrow, exhaustively-listed law-enforcement exceptions that each require prior judicial or administrative authorisation; under Article 5(5) Member States may enable those exceptions in national law and may set stricter national rules. Article 5(1)(c) carve-out: the social-scoring prohibition does not affect lawful evaluation practices of natural persons that are carried out for a specific purpose in accordance with Union and national law (Recital 31 final sentence). Article 5(1)(f) carve-out: emotion-recognition systems placed on the market strictly for medical or safety reasons, including systems intended for therapeutical use, fatigue detection in pilots/drivers for accident prevention, and pain/fatigue physical-state monitoring (which Recital 18 expressly excludes from the 'emotion' definition itself), are NOT prohibited (Recital 44 final sentence). Article 5(1)(g) carve-out: the biometric-categorisation prohibition does not cover lawful labelling, filtering or categorisation of biometric datasets acquired in line with Union or national law, including sorting by hair colour or eye colour, which is permitted in law-enforcement contexts (Recital 30). Article 5(1)(h) carve-out catalogue: real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces by law enforcement is permitted only for three exhaustive law-enforcement objectives, (i) targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking and sexual exploitation, and missing persons; (ii) prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety, or a genuine and foreseeable terrorist attack; (iii) localisation or identification of suspects of Annex II offences punishable by at least 4 years' custody. Use requires prior FRIA (Article 27), Article 49 EU-database registration, prior judicial or independent-administrative authorisation (urgency exception: authorisation within 24h, else immediate stop), and notification of the relevant market-surveillance authority and national data-protection authority. question: About obligations of transparency to providers who want to use a GPAI model, do you need to disclose: date of release? number of paramaters? applicable model interaction with hardware? license? samples of outlier data used in training? Given clear yes/no to each item.
jul07_answer: Yes to four of the five, no to the last. The transparency duty to downstream providers who intend to integrate a GPAI model is Article 53(1)(b), which requires the operator to draw up and keep current the information and documentation specified in Annex XII for those integrators. Date of release: Yes. Annex XII requires the date of release and methods of distribution as part of the general model description. Number of parameters: Yes. Annex XII requires disclosure of the model's architecture and number of parameters. Model interaction with hardware: Yes, where applicable. Annex XII requires describing how the model interacts with, or can be used to interact with, hardware or software that is not part of the model itself. License: Yes. Annex XII requires the license for the model. Samples of outlier data used in training: No. Neither Annex XII nor Article 53(1)(b) requires disclosing training-data samples to integrators. The only training-data disclosure obligation is the separate Article 53(1)(d) duty to publish a sufficiently detailed public summary of training content, and that is a general summary, not samples of outlier data.

easy.answer: Article 53(1)(b) requires a GPAI provider to draw up, keep up to date and make available to providers of AI systems who intend to integrate the model the information set out in Annex XII, and Annex XII expressly names the date of release and methods of distribution, how the model interacts with hardware or software that is not part of the model itself, the architecture and number of parameters, and the licence for the model. Annex XII asks only for information on the data used for training, testing and validation, including its type and provenance and the curation methodologies, and the separate public summary under Article 53(1)(d) is a sufficiently detailed summary of training content covering public datasets, scraped web content, user data, synthetic data and licensed content, not a release of individual or illustrative data records. Under Article 53(2) the Annex XII downstream-provider information duty, like the Annex XI technical documentation duty, does not apply to a model released under a free and open-source licence permitting access, use, modification and distribution with publicly available parameters, weights, architecture and usage information. That carve-out falls away if the model is designated as having systemic risk under Article 51 on the basis of high-impact capabilities, presumed above 10^25 FLOPs of cumulative training compute, in which case the full Article 53 duties and the Article 55 systemic-risk obligations apply regardless of licence.

Under Article 51, a GPAI model has systemic risk when cumulative training compute exceeds 10²⁵ FLOPs (10^25); providers must notify the Commission within two weeks of meeting the threshold. GPAI provider obligations: maintain technical documentation per Annex XI, supply downstream-provider information per Annex XII, implement a copyright policy, and publish a sufficiently detailed training-data summary. Where the model meets the Article 51 systemic-risk threshold (10^25 FLOPs cumulative training compute), the additional Article 55 obligations apply on top. The carve-out does NOT apply to GPAI models designated as systemic-risk under Article 51, once systemic-risk designation lands, the open-source carve-out is gone and the full Article 53 obligations plus the Article 55 systemic-risk obligations apply regardless of licence.
