Commission's 18 July 2025 GPAI Guidelines presume a model is general-purpose (Article 3(63)) when training compute exceeds 10^23 FLOPs and the model can generate language, image, audio, or video output. Fine-tuned or modified models become new providers under Article 25 when their additional training compute exceeds one-third of the base model's compute (or one-third of the 10^25 systemic threshold, ~3.3×10^24 FLOPs, when base compute is unknown). Article 10 requires training, validation, and test datasets to be relevant, representative.

question: Who, if at all, needs to establish the post-market monitoring system for a high-risk AI system? Provider/deployer/AI office? Is it possible that the monitoring system may need to also include info on interaction with other AI systems than the high-risk one in consideration?
jul07_answer: The provider must establish the post-market monitoring system for a high-risk AI system, not the deployer and not the AI Office. On the substance, Article 72 requires the provider to establish and document a post-market monitoring system proportionate to the nature of the AI technologies and the risks of the high-risk system, to collect and analyse performance data across the system's lifetime (including data provided by deployers), and to feed that back into continuous compliance with the Chapter III requirements. On the operator's second question, yes. Article 72 expressly provides that, where relevant, post-market monitoring shall include an analysis of the interaction with other AI systems. So the monitoring system may legitimately need to capture information about how the high-risk system behaves in combination with other AI systems in its operating environment, not just the high-risk system in isolation. This is a conditional element ("where relevant"): it is triggered where such interactions materially bear on the system's performance or continued compliance, and it is not a mandatory data field in every case. If you want, I can map the full Chapter IX chain (Article 72 monitoring → reporting duties) against the operator's specific system.

easy.answer: The provider must establish the post-market monitoring system, the obligation attaches to the provider alone, and neither the deployer nor the AI Office (nor the national market surveillance authority) bears it. The duty is triggered by the system's classification as high-risk under Article 6, i.e. either because it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and requires third-party conformity assessment, or because it falls within one of the Annex III use cases; absent that classification, no post-market monitoring system is required at all. It sits in a closed loop with the risk management system that, under Article 9, must be established, implemented, documented and maintained in relation to high-risk AI systems as a continuous iterative process across the lifecycle: data gathered post-market feeds back into the Article 9 risk assessment and, where necessary, into corrective action and reporting of serious incidents. Note that the specific post-market monitoring provisions (Chapter IX) are not among the provisions supplied in the reference set here, so the article numbering above is deliberately left uncited; the substantive allocation of the duty to the provider is nonetheless settled. On the second question, yes, and it is a statutory requirement rather than a matter of the provider's discretion.

hard_t1.answer: The system described is not among the practices prohibited under Article 5 (social scoring, untargeted facial-image scraping, manipulative or exploitative techniques, and the other exhaustively-listed bans). Whether it is high-risk turns on Article 6: it is high-risk only if it is a safety component of a product regulated under Annex I (for example a medical device under the MDR or IVDR) or falls within one of the Annex III use cases. Otherwise it is limited- or minimal-risk, subject mainly to the Article 50 transparency duties where it interacts directly with people.

question: What is an "area" and what is a "use case" for high-risk as per Article 6(2)? How many areas exist?
jul07_answer: An "area" under Article 6(2) is one of the broad domains listed in Annex III within which an AI system is classified high-risk, and a "use case" is a specific intended purpose within that area (a particular application the system is put to). Article 6(2) makes an AI system high-risk where it falls within one of the eight Annex III use-case categories, and each of those categories functions as an area containing one or more concrete use cases. The eight Annex III areas are: biometrics; critical infrastructure; education and vocational training; employment and worker management (covering recruitment, task allocation, promotion and termination decisions, and performance evaluation affecting workers' fundamental rights); access to essential private and public services; law enforcement; migration, asylum and border control; and administration of justice and democratic processes. This Annex III route is one of two paths to high-risk status. The other is the Annex I route under Article 6(1), which covers AI that is a safety component of, or is itself, a product under the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I where that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment. Under the Article 6(3) derogation, an Annex III system is not high-risk where it poses no significant risk of harm and performs only a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns without replacing or influencing the human assessment, or carries out a preparatory task, though it remains high-risk whenever it profiles natural persons.

easy.answer: Under Article 6(2), an "area" is one of the eight broad headings in Annex III, and a "use case" is a specific intended purpose listed under one of those headings, so a system is high-risk under that route only where its intended purpose matches a listed use case within one of the eight areas. Those areas are biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management (covering recruitment, task allocation, promotion and termination decisions, and performance evaluation affecting workers' fundamental rights), essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes (Annex III). Falling within a listed use case is not conclusive, because the Article 6(3) derogation removes an Annex III system from the high-risk tier where it poses no significant risk of harm and performs only a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, or performs a preparatory task, unless it profiles natural persons, in which case it remains high-risk. The provider must document that self-assessment before placing the system on the market and still register it under Article 49(2), which requires registration in the EU database before market placement or putting into service. The number of areas is not permanently fixed, since Article 7 empowers the Commission to amend Annex III by adding or modifying use cases, and Article 112 requires the Commission to assess annually whether the Annex III list needs amendment.

question: Name the areas of high-risk use cases. Is healthcare decision making one of them?
jul07_answer: Healthcare clinical decision-making is not itself one of the enumerated Annex III use-case areas, though medical AI is still routinely high-risk through the separate Annex I route. Under Article 6(2), the eight Annex III use-case categories are biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration and asylum and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes (Annex III). Medical AI instead typically becomes high-risk under the Annex I route in Article 6(1), which classifies a system as high-risk where it is, or is a safety component of, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment. Annex I lists medical devices, so an AI system functioning as a medical device or as a safety component of one is captured on this basis. Article 43(3) then integrates the AI Act assessment into the sectoral procedure, so a medical device runs a single conformity assessment through its MDR notified body covering both regimes. One Annex III category can also reach the health sector at its access layer: essential private and public services covers AI used to evaluate eligibility for essential healthcare services, which is distinct from the clinical judgement that the Annex I medical-device route addresses.

easy.answer: Not as a standalone Annex III area, but healthcare decision making is usually high-risk by the other classification route. Article 6(2) classifies a system as high-risk where it falls within one of the eight Annex III use cases, which are biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, access to essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes. Clinical decision making instead engages the Annex I route in Article 6(1), under which a system is high-risk where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation. Annex I Section A lists medical devices, so AI functioning as or within a medical device is high-risk on that basis. Article 43(3) then integrates the AI Act assessment into the sectoral third-party conformity assessment, meaning the MDR notified-body procedure covers both regimes in one procedure. The Article 6(3) derogation removes an Annex III system from the high-risk tier where it poses no significant risk of harm and performs only a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, or performs a preparatory task, but it never applies where the system profiles natural persons, and it does not apply to the Annex I route at all. Article 7 also empowers the Commission to add, modify or remove Annex III use cases by delegated act, using criteria including intended purpose, impact on health, safety and fundamental rights, and the severity and reversibility of harm.

question: What does Annex VII point 5.1 say? Try to get the substance right. Do not get confused with other material, like 5.1 in Annex III or Article 7, which is about something else entirely.
jul07_answer: Annex VII point 5.1 falls under the heading "Changes to the AI system." It requires that any change to the high-risk AI system which could affect its compliance with the requirements of the Regulation, or its intended purpose, be approved by the notified body that issued the EU technical-documentation assessment certificate. In other words, once the notified body has audited the quality management system and examined the technical documentation and issued that certificate under the Annex VII procedure, the provider cannot unilaterally alter the system in a way that touches conformity or intended purpose. The provider must notify the notified body, which reassesses the change, and any approval takes the form of a supplement to the original assessment certificate. This is distinct from Annex III point 5 (essential private and public services as a high-risk use case) and from Article 7 (the Commission's delegated-act power to amend the Annex III list), which address entirely different subject matter.

easy.answer: Annex VII point 5.1 states the purpose of the surveillance stage of that conformity assessment procedure, namely to make sure that the provider duly fulfils the terms and conditions of the approved quality management system. It opens the ongoing supervision part of Annex VII, which follows the notified body's approval of the quality management system and its examination of the technical documentation, the procedure that applies under Annex VII to Annex III biometric systems where harmonised standards have not been fully applied and which ends in an EU technical documentation assessment certificate. The system being supervised is the quality management system that Article 17 requires providers of high-risk AI systems to put in place to ensure compliance with the Regulation. It is unrelated to the criteria in Article 7 for adding, modifying or removing high-risk use cases in Annex III by delegated act, and unrelated to the Annex III use-case headings themselves.

question: Do providers of GPAI systems, even if not with systemic risk, have an obligation to extensively shield their models from adversarial attacks? What about specifically for adversarial images? What about specifically for prompt injection?
jul07_answer: The obligations that attach to a non-systemic-risk GPAI provider under Article 53 are limited to maintaining technical documentation (Annex XI), supplying integration information to downstream providers (Annex XII), putting in place a copyright policy, and publishing a training-data summary. None of these requires adversarial hardening. The demanding adversarial-testing and cybersecurity duties sit in Article 55, which imposes state-of-the-art model evaluation including documented adversarial red-teaming and an adequate level of cybersecurity protection only on GPAI models with systemic risk (presumed above 10^25 FLOPs of cumulative training compute). Those Article 55 duties do not reach a model below that threshold. The resilience-against-adversarial-attacks duty in Article 15, which requires appropriate robustness and resistance to evasion, data-poisoning, and adversarial attacks, is framed for high-risk AI systems, not for GPAI models as such. Adversarial images: no distinct obligation. The Act sets no image-specific defensive duty for a non-systemic-risk GPAI provider. Resistance to adversarial or evasion inputs, which would include perturbed images, arises only through Article 15 robustness where the model operates within a high-risk AI system, or through Article 55 adversarial testing where the model carries systemic risk. Prompt injection: no distinct obligation. Likewise there is no prompt-injection-specific requirement for a non-systemic-risk GPAI provider.

easy.answer: No. A provider of a GPAI model without systemic risk has no general obligation to harden the model against adversarial attacks, because the obligations in Article 53 that apply to all GPAI providers are documentary rather than security-related: technical documentation of the training, testing and evaluation process per Annex XI, information for downstream providers integrating the model per Annex XII, a policy to comply with Union copyright law, and a publicly available summary of the training content. The duties to conduct and document adversarial testing, to assess and mitigate systemic risks at Union level, to report serious incidents, and to ensure an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure arise only under Article 55, which is triggered by the Article 51 classification as a model with systemic risk (presumed above 10^25 FLOPs of cumulative training compute or designated by the Commission on the Annex XIII criteria). Where a model does fall under Article 55, adversarial images and prompt injection would be handled as part of the state-of-the-art adversarial testing and cybersecurity obligations rather than as separate requirements, and a provider may rely on the Article 56 codes of practice, which the AI Office facilitates as a means of demonstrating compliance until a harmonised standard is published. Note also that the Article 53(2) carve-out for free and open-source releases removes only the Annex XI and Annex XII documentation duties, so it changes nothing about security obligations either way.

hard_t1.answer: Under Article 53, GPAI providers must maintain Annex XI documentation, supply downstream-provider information, and publish a training-data summary; the Article 53(2) carve-out means each documentation obligation does not apply to free and open-source models below the systemic threshold. Under Article 51, a GPAI model has systemic risk when cumulative training compute exceeds 10²⁵ FLOPs (10^25); providers must notify the Commission within two weeks of meeting the threshold. Under Article 56, Codes of Practice by the AI Office offer a route for GPAI providers to demonstrate Article 53 and 55 compliance; signing is voluntary, and providers may use any alternative adequate means to demonstrate compliance. Article 53(2) free / open-source carve-out: the Annex XI technical-documentation obligation and the Annex XII downstream-provider information obligation under Article 53(1)(a)-(b) do NOT apply to GPAI models released under a free and open-source licence permitting access, use, modification and distribution, with publicly available parameters (weights, architecture and usage information). The carve-out does NOT apply to GPAI models designated as systemic-risk under Article 51, once systemic-risk designation lands, the open-source carve-out is gone and the full Article 53 obligations plus the Article 55 systemic-risk obligations apply regardless of licence. The Article 53(1)(c) copyright policy and the Article 53(1)(d) public training-data summary apply to ALL GPAI providers including open-source releases. Article 55 adds four obligations on top of Article 53 for GPAI providers with systemic risk: (a) model evaluation in accordance with standardised protocols and tools reflecting the state of the art, including conducting and documenting adversarial testing to identify and mitigate systemic risks; (b) assess and mitigate possible systemic risks at Union level, including their sources, that may stem from development, market-placement, or use of the model; (c) keep track of, document, and report without undue delay to the AI Office (and national competent authorities where appropriate) information about serious incidents and possible corrective measures; (d) ensure an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for both the model AND its physical infrastructure. Providers may rely on Article 56 codes of practice to demonstrate compliance until a harmonised standard is published. Classifies a general-purpose AI model as having 'systemic risk' when it has high-impact capabilities (presumed when cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs) or when so designated by the Commission based on Annex XIII criteria. Commission's 18 July 2025 GPAI Guidelines presume a model is general-purpose (Article 3(63)) when training compute exceeds 10^23 FLOPs and the model can generate language, image, audio, or video output. Fine-tuned or modified models become new providers under Article 25 when their additional training compute exceeds one-third of the base model's compute (or one-third of the 10^25 systemic threshold, ~3.3×10^24 FLOPs, when base compute is unknown).

question: Could the introduction of guardrails in an AI agentic system reduce the risk of the system from high risk to moderate risk? What about changing the capabilities and intended use of the system?
jul07_answer: Whether a system is high-risk is fixed by Article 6, which classifies a system as high-risk either where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Annex I harmonisation legislation requiring third-party conformity assessment, or where it falls within one of the eight Annex III use cases. Guardrails are risk-control measures within the risk-management system that Article 9 requires across the lifecycle, including mitigation of foreseeable and misuse risks. Under the Article 6(3) derogation, an Annex III system is not high-risk where it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and performs only a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, or carries out a preparatory task. The provider must document that self-assessment before placing the system on the market and still register it under Article 49(2). Under Article 25(1), a deployer or third party who makes a substantial modification or modifies the intended purpose is treated as a provider and assumes the full provider obligations, and a modification that makes a system high-risk pulls it into the regime rather than out of it. So a change of use only lowers exposure where it moves the system into the Article 6(3) conditions, and the same lever can raise exposure if it points the other way.

easy.answer: Guardrails are risk-control measures under Article 9, which requires a documented, iterative risk-management system identifying foreseeable risks, estimating risks emerging during misuse, and adopting targeted mitigation. They reduce residual risk but do not move the system out of the high-risk tier, because Article 8 requires compliance with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements by reference to the system's intended purpose and the state of the art, and Annex III fixes the high-risk use-case categories (biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration and asylum and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes). Guardrails therefore serve as evidence of adequate risk control, and their operation and limits must be reflected in the Article 13 instructions for use, which must state capabilities and limitations and the known or foreseeable circumstances that may lead to risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, and in the Article 12 automatic logs, which must give traceability appropriate to the intended purpose and be retained for at least six months. Narrowing the capabilities and intended purpose can change the outcome, but only where the redefined intended purpose genuinely falls outside the Annex III categories and outside any Article 7 addition made by delegated act, in which case the Chapter III Section 2 obligations cease to apply and only the Article 50 transparency duties may remain, such as disclosing the system's AI nature to natural persons interacting with it and marking synthetic content in a machine-readable format. Note also that under Article 25(1) a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party that modifies the intended purpose, or makes a substantial modification, becomes a provider and assumes the full provider obligations, and the same rule operates in reverse where a modification of intended purpose makes a system high-risk.

question: Can law enforcement starts using a real-time remote biometric identification system without prior authorisation? If yes, how much time do they have to seek authorisation, and what happens if the authorisation is refused?
jul07_answer: Yes, but only in a duly justified situation of urgency. Real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement is prohibited under Article 5 except for the narrow, exhaustively listed exceptions, each of which normally requires prior judicial or administrative authorisation. Where urgency justifies it, law enforcement may begin using the system before that authorisation is granted, provided they request the authorisation without undue delay and at the latest within 24 hours of the start of use. If the requested authorisation is refused, the use must be stopped with immediate effect and all data, outputs and results of that use must be discarded and deleted. This all operates within the Article 5(5) framework, under which Member States may choose to enable these exceptions in national law and may impose stricter national rules. Outside the prohibited real-time law-enforcement scenario, biometric identification systems are not banned but fall to be treated as high-risk under Article 6 and Annex III, which lists biometrics among the eight high-risk use-case categories.

easy.answer: Yes, but only in a duly justified situation of urgency, and only where the use falls within one of the exhaustively listed law enforcement exceptions to the Article 5 prohibition on real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces. In that case authorisation must be requested without undue delay and at the latest within 24 hours of the start of the use. If the authorisation is refused, the use must be stopped with immediate effect and all data, results and output of that use must be deleted and discarded. Outside those exceptions the practice remains a prohibited practice under Article 5, and Article 5(5) leaves Member States free to decide whether to enable the exceptions in national law at all and to adopt stricter national rules. Where the use is permitted, the system is regulated at the second tier rather than banned. Remote biometric identification falls within the biometrics and law enforcement categories of Annex III and is therefore high-risk under the Article 6(2) route, the law enforcement authority deploying it must carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment covering the deployment process, affected persons, specific risks, human oversight measures and complaints workflows before first use under Article 27, and as a public authority deployer it must register itself and the system in the EU database under Article 49 before putting it into service.

hard_t1.answer: Under Article 5.1.h, real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces by law-enforcement authorities is prohibited; narrow exceptions require prior judicial or independent-administrative authorization, an Article 27 fundamental-rights impact assessment, and Article 49 EU-database registration. Real-time remote biometric identification by law enforcement is prohibited under Article 5 save for narrow, exhaustively-listed law-enforcement exceptions that each require prior judicial or administrative authorisation; under Article 5(5) Member States may enable those exceptions in national law and may set stricter national rules. Eight high-risk use-case categories: biometrics, critical infrastructure, education + vocational training, employment + worker management (recruitment, task allocation, promotion and termination decisions, and performance evaluation affecting workers' fundamental rights), essential private + public services, law enforcement, migration + asylum + border control, and administration of justice + democratic processes. Deployers of certain high-risk AI systems (Annex III + public-sector deployers) must perform a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment before first use, covering deployment process, affected persons, specific risks, human-oversight measures, and complaints workflows.

question: Consider a private contractor of the municipality that runs a city's emergency-call triage platform. The contractor plans to use an AI tool to prioritize police response decisions. Before going live with the system, does this contractor need to look into fundamental rights impact assessment (FRIA)? Is this because of this scenario belonging to Annex III 5(b) or 5(c)? What about private contractors offering other public services concerning Annex III but NOT specifically 5(b) or 5(c)?
jul07_answer: Yes, the contractor must run a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment before going live, but not because of Annex III point 5(b) or 5(c). Emergency-call triage that dispatches police sits within Annex III's essential public services category (point 5(d) on emergency first-response dispatching), not the creditworthiness scoring of 5(b) or the life-and-health insurance risk-and-pricing of 5(c). Under Article 6(2), any system falling within an Annex III use case is high-risk, and Article 27 then obliges the relevant deployers to assess the system's impact on fundamental rights before first use, covering the deployment process, affected persons, specific risks, human-oversight measures, and complaints workflows. The reason this obligation reaches the contractor is that Article 27 extends the FRIA duty to private operators providing a public service, which is exactly what a municipal emergency-triage contractor is. Points 5(b) and 5(c) serve a separate function in Article 27. For private contractors delivering other public services within Annex III, the public-service-provider limb is what applies. They must perform the FRIA whenever they deploy a high-risk Annex III system in the course of providing that public service, regardless of whether the use case is 5(b) or 5(c). The one carve-out to keep in view is that Article 27's FRIA duty does not attach to the Annex III critical-infrastructure category, so a public-service contractor operating there would not be caught by this obligation on that basis.

easy.answer: Yes, a fundamental rights impact assessment is required, but not by reason of Annex III points 5(b) or 5(c). Those two points concern creditworthiness evaluation and risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance. A system that evaluates and classifies emergency calls and prioritises the dispatch of emergency first response services, including police, sits at Annex III point 5(d) inside the essential private and public services category, which makes it high-risk on the Annex III route of Article 6(2). Article 27(1) obliges deployers of Article 6(2) high-risk systems to assess the impact on fundamental rights before first use, addressing the deployment process, the categories of persons likely to be affected, the specific risks of harm, the human oversight measures and the internal complaints workflow, and it captures this contractor because a private entity running a municipal emergency service is providing a public service. The Article 6(3) derogation is not available here, since prioritising police response is neither a narrow procedural nor a preparatory task, and the system profiles natural persons, which keeps it high-risk in any event. The public service limb of Article 27 is not confined to points 5(b) and 5(c). A private contractor deploying any other Annex III high-risk system in the delivery of a public service owes the same assessment, the one exception being systems intended for use in the critical infrastructure area of Annex III point 2.

hard_t1.answer: Deployers of certain high-risk AI systems (Annex III + public-sector deployers) must perform a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment before first use, covering deployment process, affected persons, specific risks, human-oversight measures, and complaints workflows. Classifies an AI system as high-risk on two routes. Annex I route (Article 6(1)): the system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I AND that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation. Annex III route (Article 6(2)): the system falls within one of the eight Annex III use cases. Article 6(3) derogation: an Annex III system is NOT high-risk where it poses no significant risk of harm and meets one of four conditions (a narrow procedural task; improving the result of a previously completed human activity; detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment; or a preparatory task), unless it profiles natural persons, in which case it is always high-risk; the provider must document this self-assessment before placing the system on the market and still register it under Article 49(2).

question: Is the use of deep-fake images in university classes to represent e.g. skin conditions in patients allowed? Does the artificial nature of the content need to be disclosed for such an evidently educational and illustrative use? If so, does the lighter transparency requirement apply like for certain law enforcement situations?
jul07_answer: No. Under Article 50(4), the deployer's duty to disclose that image, audio, or video content constituting a deep fake has been artificially generated or manipulated does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate, or prosecute criminal offences. Absent that law-enforcement authorisation, the deployer must disclose that the content is a deep fake.

easy.answer: No. Under Article 50(4), the deployer's duty to disclose that image, audio, or video content constituting a deep fake has been artificially generated or manipulated does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate, or prosecute criminal offences. Absent that law-enforcement authorisation, the deployer must disclose that the content is a deep fake.

hard_t1.answer: No. Under Article 50(4), the deployer's duty to disclose that image, audio, or video content constituting a deep fake has been artificially generated or manipulated does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate, or prosecute criminal offences. Absent that law-enforcement authorisation, the deployer must disclose that the content is a deep fake.

question: If a high-risk AI system was already placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2026, does the AI Act fully apply to it? What about general purpose AI systems?
jul07_answer: Not fully, a high-risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2026 is largely grandfathered and becomes subject to the Act only if, after that date, it undergoes significant changes in its design. Absent a significant design change, the full high-risk obligation set does not attach retroactively to the existing deployment. General-purpose AI models follow a separate transitional track: those placed on the market before 2 August 2025 are not exempt but are given until 2 August 2027 to be brought into compliance with the GPAI provisions (Chapter V, Articles 51 to 56), the provider being obliged in the interim to take the necessary steps to conform by that date. So neither legacy high-risk systems nor pre-existing GPAI models are subject to immediate full application on 2 August 2026, the former turn on the "significant change" trigger (with the 2030 backstop for public-authority use), and the latter on the fixed 2 August 2027 deadline. One caveat on terminology: the Act regulates general-purpose AI models (Articles 51 to 56), not "general-purpose AI systems" as such; a system built on a GPAI model is classified on its own facts under Article 6, and if it is not a safety component of an Annex I product and does not fall within an Annex III use case, it is limited- or minimal-risk and subject mainly to the Article 50 transparency duties rather than the high-risk transitional rules above.

easy.answer: What the grandfathering does not do is alter classification. A legacy system remains high-risk under Article 6 on whichever route qualified it, a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, or a use case within one of the Annex III categories such as biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, or employment and worker management, so a significant change in design after 2 August 2026 activates the full Chapter III regime, including the risk management system under Article 9, for a system whose classification never changed. Nor does the carve-out displace the Article 50 transparency obligations, which attach to providers by reference to the system's direct interaction with natural persons and to the marking of synthetic AI-generated content in a machine-readable, detectable format, independently of the high-risk tier. The prohibitions in Article 5 likewise carry no transitional relief: a practice banned under that Article, and the boundary matters, since emotion recognition placed on the market strictly for medical or safety reasons, such as therapeutical use or fatigue detection in pilots and drivers for accident prevention, falls outside the ban and is instead assessed as high-risk under has been unlawful since the prohibitions became applicable, whenever the system was first placed on the market.

hard_t1.answer: The system described is not among the practices prohibited under Article 5 (social scoring, untargeted facial-image scraping, manipulative or exploitative techniques, and the other exhaustively-listed bans). Whether it is high-risk turns on Article 6: it is high-risk only if it is a safety component of a product regulated under Annex I (for example a medical device under the MDR or IVDR) or falls within one of the Annex III use cases. Otherwise it is limited- or minimal-risk, subject mainly to the Article 50 transparency duties where it interacts directly with people.

question: What is Annex X about? What is it used for?
jul07_answer: Annex X is the schedule that lists exactly which data must be entered in the EU database when a high-risk AI system is registered. It supports the registration duty in Article 49, which obliges providers (and public-authority deployers) to register themselves and the system in the EU database (Article 71) before it is placed on the market or put into service. The required entries include the identity and contact details of the provider, authorised representative and deployer, the system name, trade name and an unambiguous reference, its intended purpose, and its market status (on the market, in service, withdrawn or recalled). Providers must also enter the type and number of any conformity-assessment certificate and the notified body that issued it, the Member States where the system is available, and a copy of the EU declaration of conformity drawn up under Article 47 together with the instructions for use. Annex X also carves out systems used for law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control, whose registration entries are not made publicly accessible.

easy.answer: Annex X sets out the information that must be entered in the EU database when a high-risk AI system is registered. It applies to providers, to authorised representatives where applicable, and to deployers that are public authorities, all of whom Article 49 requires to register themselves and the system in the EU database maintained under Article 71 before the system is placed on the market or put into service. The required entries are the registrant's identity and contact details, the system name, trade name and any additional unambiguous reference, the intended purpose, the status of the system (placed on the market, in service, no longer placed on the market, or recalled), the type and number of the conformity assessment certificate and the identity of the issuing notified body where applicable, the Member States in which the system is placed on the market or put into service, a copy of the EU declaration of conformity that Article 47 requires the provider to draw up in written, machine-readable, signed and dated form for each high-risk AI system, and the instructions for use. Annex X also contains public-access carve-outs, so the corresponding entries for law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control systems are not made publicly accessible.

question: A supermarket uses an AI tool that analyzes only current-cart and checkout anomalies (no biometrics, no face recognition, no sensitive-trait inference, no cross-context social scoring) to flag transactions for optional manual bag checks by store staff. The retailer claims this is "high risk like policing", as it: resembles investigation of potentially criminal offences (theft) + evaluates or classifies persons based on observed behaviour in a way that may lead to detrimental or unfavourable treatment. Is this situation potentially high-risk?
jul07_answer: Not high-risk, and not prohibited. Single-transaction anomaly detection that flags a cart for an optional manual bag check by store staff falls outside both the Article 5(1)(c) social-scoring prohibition and the law-enforcement high-risk category, because the two facts the retailer relies on do not satisfy the statutory tests. Article 5(1)(c) prohibits only systems that evaluate or classify natural persons over time on the basis of social behaviour or personal characteristics, where the resulting score produces detrimental treatment in unrelated social contexts or treatment that is unjustified or disproportionate; here the system assesses a single present transaction (current cart and checkout anomalies), not accumulated behaviour over time, and any consequence, a bag check at that same till, arises within the very transactional context that generated the signal, not an unrelated one, so neither the temporal-scoring element nor the context-transfer element of the prohibition is met. This verdict holds so long as those facts remain true, it would require reassessment only if the tool were in fact deployed by or for a law-enforcement authority, or extended to profile identified individuals across visits over time in a way that drives disadvantage beyond the immediate transaction.

easy.answer: A supermarket AI tool that analyses only current-cart and checkout anomalies to flag transactions for optional manual bag checks by store staff is not high-risk and not a prohibited practice on the facts described, and would become high-risk only where the retailer deploys it by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, which would engage the Annex III law enforcement classification under Article 6(2). The retailer's social scoring theory fails on the cumulative conditions of Article 5(1)(c), which requires evaluation or classification of natural persons over a period of time on the basis of social behaviour or known, inferred or predicted personal characteristics, and a resulting detrimental or unfavourable treatment either in social contexts unrelated to the contexts in which the data was originally generated or that is unjustified or disproportionate to the gravity of the behaviour. The predictive policing prohibition in Article 5(1)(d) likewise does not attach, as it targets the assessment or prediction of the risk of a natural person committing a criminal offence based solely on profiling or on assessing personality traits and characteristics, and expressly preserves AI used to support a human assessment grounded in objective and verifiable facts directly linked to a criminal activity; a checkout anomaly signal reviewed by staff is of that character, and the offences in Annex II are not in issue. Article 4 AI literacy obligations apply irrespective of tier.

hard_t1.answer: Social scoring is prohibited under Article 5(1)(c): AI systems that evaluate or classify natural persons over time based on their social behaviour or personal characteristics, where the resulting score leads to detrimental or unfavourable treatment in unrelated social contexts, or to treatment that is unjustified or disproportionate. The prohibition binds any provider or deployer, public or private, regardless of deployment context.

question: We are a private educational institution intending to deploy an AI tool that analyses students' prior grades and learning outcomes to recommend whether they should follow the standard or accelerated honours track going forward. We remark that a student who receives the "standard" recommendation is *not* barred from choosing accelerated, the system merely provides a suggestion. Are there reasons to believe the system might be high-risk? What articles/annex and specific points, if any, concern this use case?
jul07_answer: A system that profiles students' prior grades and learning outcomes to recommend a standard versus accelerated honours track is likely high-risk, because it falls within the education and vocational-training use case listed in Annex III and is therefore classified as high-risk under the second route of Article 6 (Article 6(2)), which designates an AI system as high-risk where it is intended to be used within one of the Annex III categories. The Annex III education category captures precisely this function, AI intended to evaluate learning outcomes and to steer a person's assignment or access to an educational or vocational track, and the operative test is the purpose of the system, not the formal bindingness of its output. Article 6 does provide a filter under which a system that would otherwise fall within Annex III is not high-risk where it performs only a narrow procedural task or does not materially influence the outcome of a decision affecting the person; but a system that assesses a student's record and produces a track recommendation is doing exactly the substantive evaluative and steering work that the education category is meant to reach, and an advisory output that shapes how a student, teacher, or institution channels that student still materially influences the educational trajectory. Unless the operator can substantiate that the tool performs only a narrow ancillary function and does not meaningfully influence which track is taken, it remains high-risk under Article 6(2) via the burden of establishing that derogation rests on the operator and should be documented. This is a high-risk classification, not a prohibited practice: Article 5 bans a closed list of practices (subliminal or manipulative techniques causing significant harm and the exploitation of vulnerabilities arising from age, disability, or socio-economic situation, among the eight categories), and a grade-based track-recommendation tool does not, on the facts described, deploy manipulative or exploitative techniques of that kind, so Article 5 is not engaged. The other high-risk route in Article 6 (Article 6(1)) does not apply either, since the system is not a safety component of a product regulated under Annex I harmonisation legislation. As a deployer of a high-risk system, note that the Chapter III provider obligations (risk management, data governance, technical documentation, and the rest) attach primarily to the provider, while distinct deployer duties arise on top of the high-risk designation; and where the system interacts directly with students, the Article 50 transparency duty to disclose its AI nature applies independently of the high-risk status.

easy.answer: The classification arises under Article 6, which routes a system into the high-risk tier where it falls within one of the use cases listed in Annex III; the applicable category here is Annex III, point 3 on education and vocational training, and specifically point 3(c), covering systems intended to assess the appropriate level of education that a natural person will receive or will be able to access. Annex III attaches to the intended purpose of the system rather than to the formal bindingness of its result, and a recommendation that channels a student toward or away from an accelerated track is in substance an assessment of the level of education that student will access. The derogation in Article 6(3), under which an Annex III system may escape the high-risk tier where it performs only a narrow procedural task, a preparatory task, or an improvement on a previously completed human activity, is also unavailable: a system that scores individual students on the basis of their personal academic history performs profiling of natural persons, and Article 6(3) provides that such a system is in all cases to be considered high-risk. Article 5 operates at a different level and is not engaged. A practice is prohibited under that Article where it deploys subliminal, purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques (Article 5(1)(a)), or exploits vulnerabilities arising from age, disability, or a specific socio-economic situation (Article 5(1)(b)), so as to materially distort behaviour and cause significant harm. A track recommendation derived from recorded academic performance does not meet that threshold, and the system therefore sits within the high-risk tier rather than the prohibited one; it would cross into Article 5(1)(b) only if it were designed to exploit students' socio-economic situation in a manner materially distorting their choices to their significant detriment. As deployer of an Annex III system, note additionally that Article 27 requires a fundamental rights impact assessment prior to deployment for deployers that are bodies governed by public law and for private entities providing public services; whether the operator's institution falls within that scope turns on whether the education it delivers constitutes a public service in the relevant Member State. Annex I is not in issue, as the system is not a safety component of a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation.

hard_t1.answer: The system described is not among the practices prohibited under Article 5 (social scoring, untargeted facial-image scraping, manipulative or exploitative techniques, and the other exhaustively-listed bans). Whether it is high-risk turns on Article 6: it is high-risk only if it is a safety component of a product regulated under Annex I (for example a medical device under the MDR or IVDR) or falls within one of the Annex III use cases. Otherwise it is limited- or minimal-risk, subject mainly to the Article 50 transparency duties where it interacts directly with people.

question: We manufactured an industrial robot with an embedded AI module that decides when to reduce speed near human workers to prevent hurting them. The robot is covered by the Machinery Regulation, listed in Annex I of the AI Act. We already underwent conformity assessment with a notified body and got a CE mark for the robot. Do we need the AI module undergo a separate AI Act conformity assessment dedicated to the AI Act? Do we need to submit the system to the EU database of high-risk AI systems?
jul07_answer: No separate, standalone AI Act conformity assessment is required, but the AI Act requirements must be covered within the operator's existing procedure. The operator's AI module is a safety component of a product covered by the Machinery Regulation listed in Annex I, which classifies it as high-risk under Article 6(1). Under Article 43(3), the AI Act conformity assessment is integrated into the third-party conformity assessment already required under the sectoral Machinery legislation, so both regimes are discharged through one single procedure rather than a second dedicated AI Act track. This does not automatically mean the CE mark you already hold satisfies the AI Act. The notified-body procedure must actually have examined the AI module against the AI Act obligations, not only the Machinery Regulation ones. If the operator's completed assessment did not cover the AI Act requirements, that single integrated procedure must be extended to include them. Note also that any substantial modification to the module would trigger a fresh conformity assessment under Article 43(4). On registration: yes. The module is a high-risk AI system, and the Commission maintains an EU database of high-risk AI systems under Article 71 in which such systems are registered. That registration obligation applies independently of the fact that the conformity assessment itself is folded into the Machinery procedure.

easy.answer: No on both counts, subject to one condition on the assessment you have already completed. The speed reduction module is a safety component of machinery, and machinery is Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, so the module is high-risk under Article 6(1) precisely because the product it is built into must undergo third-party conformity assessment. Article 43(3) integrates the AI Act assessment into that sectoral third-party procedure, meaning the notified body route you followed is the single procedure covering both regimes rather than a first step to be followed by a dedicated AI Act assessment. The condition is that the notified body must actually have examined the AI Act requirements for the module within that procedure, and where it did not, the assessment has to be reopened with the notified body so that the CE marking genuinely covers the AI Act as well. Under Article 43(4), a fresh conformity assessment is also required if the module is substantially modified. As to registration, the Article 71 EU database, set up and managed by the Commission with public and restricted access sections, covers high-risk systems registered under Articles 49 and 60, and that registration duty attaches to Annex III systems, including those a provider documents as not high-risk under the Article 6(3) derogation, so a safety component of an Annex I product falls outside it.

hard_t1.answer: Union harmonisation legislation list (Section A: New Legislative Framework, machinery, toys, radio equipment, medical devices, lifts, etc.; Section B: civil aviation, motor vehicles, marine equipment, rail, agricultural vehicles), AI safety-components of products covered here are classified high-risk under Article 6(1). Requires providers of high-risk AI to undergo a conformity assessment: internal-control procedure (Annex VI) for Annex-III systems where harmonised standards / common specifications are applied, otherwise notified-body procedure (Annex VII); for Annex-I products, Article 43(3) integrates the AI Act assessment into the sectoral third-party conformity-assessment procedure (for a medical device, the MDR notified-body assessment), one single procedure covering both regimes. Conformity assessment based on assessment of QMS + technical documentation with notified-body involvement: applies to Annex-III biometric systems when harmonised standards aren't fully applied, notified body audits QMS, examines technical documentation, issues EU technical-documentation assessment certificate.

question: We developed a product listed in Annex I where an AI system is a safety component. We had the option to opt out of the third-party conformity assessment base case by using harmonized standards. Thus no third-party conformity assessment happened. This means we can skip the requirements of Chapter 3 Section 2 of the AI Act, right?
jul07_answer: Union harmonisation legislation list (Section A: New Legislative Framework, machinery, toys, radio equipment, medical devices, lifts, etc.; Section B: civil aviation, motor vehicles, marine equipment, rail, agricultural vehicles), AI safety-components of products covered here are classified high-risk under Article 6(1). Annex I route (Article 6(1)): the system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I AND that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation. Annex III route (Article 6(2)): the system falls within one of the eight Annex III use cases. Article 6(3) derogation: an Annex III system is NOT high-risk where it poses no significant risk of harm and meets one of four conditions (a narrow procedural task; improving the result of a previously completed human activity; detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment; or a preparatory task), unless it profiles natural persons, in which case it is always high-risk; the provider must document this self-assessment before placing the system on the market and still register it under Article 49(2).

easy.answer: Article 6(1) classifies an AI system as high-risk on the Annex I route only where two conditions are met together: the system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I (Section A New Legislative Framework instruments such as machinery, toys, radio equipment, medical devices and lifts, and Section B instruments covering civil aviation, motor vehicles, marine equipment, rail and agricultural vehicles), and that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation. Where full application of harmonised standards lawfully makes an internal-control route available under the sectoral instrument, the second condition is not satisfied and the Annex I route does not classify the system as high-risk. The operator should still verify the independent Annex III route in Article 6(2), under which a system is high-risk if it falls within one of the eight use-case categories (biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes). If that route applies, Article 43 requires a conformity assessment based on internal control under Annex VI where harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied, and otherwise the notified-body procedure under Annex VII, and Article 43(4) requires a fresh assessment on any substantial modification.

question: A private contractor runs a region's gas supply service on behalf of the local government. It licenses an AI system from a vendor, fine-tunes it on local data, and then puts it into service under its own brand. To learn about correct applicable classifications of the system and the contractor, what material of the AI Act should I read? Does fundamental rights impact assessment (FRIA) applies?
jul07_answer: To classify both the system and the contractor, read Article 25 on responsibilities along the AI value chain together with Article 6 on high-risk classification. Because a region's gas supply is critical infrastructure, an AI system operating that service falls to be assessed as high-risk under Article 6. Article 25 then fixes the contractor's status: by putting its own brand on the licensed system and fine-tuning it on local data (a substantial modification), the contractor is treated as a provider and assumes the full provider obligations, not merely a deployer's. It also remains the deployer that puts the system into service, so both roles attach to it at once. Yes, a fundamental rights impact assessment applies. Article 27 requires deployers that are bodies governed by public law, or private operators delivering a public service, to carry out a FRIA before first use of a high-risk system, covering the deployment process, the persons affected, the specific risks, and the human-oversight measures. Running the region's gas supply on behalf of the local government is such a public service, so the contractor must complete that assessment before putting the system into service.

easy.answer: Article 27, which requires deployers that are bodies governed by public law or private entities providing public services to assess the deployment process, the categories of persons affected, the specific risks and the human oversight measures before first use, expressly carves out high-risk systems used in the area listed in point 2 of Annex III, which is the critical infrastructure heading covering safety components in the management and operation of the supply of gas. The contractor's status as a private entity performing a public service therefore does not pull it into Article 27 for this system. For the classification questions, the material to read is Article 6 together with Annex III, which set out when a system is high-risk and place safety components in critical infrastructure in point 2. For the contractor's own status, read Article 25 on responsibilities along the AI value chain, under which a party that puts a licensed system into service under its own name or trademark, or substantially modifies it, becomes the provider and assumes the full set of provider obligations, including the documented risk management system of Article 9, the technical documentation of Article 11, the conformity assessment of Article 43 and the EU database registration of Article 49. Because the contractor also operates the system in service, Article 26 remains relevant, requiring use in accordance with the instructions, human oversight by competent and trained natural persons, monitoring of operation and retention of automatically generated logs.

hard_t1.answer: Under Article 27, in addition to Article 26 baseline duties, deployers of certain Annex III high-risk AI systems must perform a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA) covering affected persons and specific fundamental rights risks. Under Article 50, limited-risk transparency: AI systems interacting with natural persons must disclose AI nature; emotion-recognition and biometric-categorisation systems must inform exposed persons; deepfakes and AI-generated content must be labelled. This system is classified as limited-risk under the Article 50 transparency obligations. The provider must provide AI literacy training to all staff involved in development, deployment and operation of the system, and document a classification assessment confirming the system is not high-risk under Article 6 (Article 4 requires providers and deployers to take measures to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among their staff and other persons dealing with AI systems on their behalf, considering technical knowledge, experience, education, training, and context of use.). A clear notice must be displayed to users at the first interaction informing them they are interacting with an AI system, and AI-generated content must be clearly labelled as such (Article 50).
